rv.q: The best of Broadway will be remembered for this one.
In its blending of modern and traditional storytelling, its poetic imagery and primal emotion, this is the kind of magical theater event that comes along only rarely.
The Broadway transfer of this London hit about a boy and his beloved horse during World War I is a theatrical experience that transcends drama to become something closer to a spiritual event.
“War Horse” isn’t sentimental: It’s just not afraid to be emotional.
The part itself lacks a compelling core, and so the musical, like the young flimflam man, remains an empty shell.
War Horse is a triumph of stagecraft over sentiment.
Nothing on screen could replicate the specific thrill of watching Joey take on substance and soul, out of disparate artificial parts, before our eyes.
What it won't have, by definition, is the direct appeal to the imagination of three people bringing a skeletal structure to animated life.
The more horselike the puppet became, the more puppetlike I found the human actors.
War Horse will make you believe that puppets live and breathe, and perhaps even have souls.
You'll leave the theater emotionally spent but exhilarated.
Joey is proof, in a season and a community in which it is urgently needed, that theatre at its simplest can still incite, inspire, and enliven as no other art form can.

The show uses 35 actors and moves from the green fields of Southwest England to the war in Northern France with a bravura visual sweep that's so inherently cinematic it seduced Steven Spielberg, whose “War Horse” movie comes out at the end of this year.
His vivid performance is rigorously honest, with a breathtaking emotional transparency.
The evocative message of War Horse lingers: Even as we seek to slaughter our foes with ever more ruthless efficiency, we need not lose our humanity.
Such sequences as when the British officer is literally blown off his steed by a flying projectile and another in which Joey is confronted by a menacing tank are staged with a nightmarish intensity.

cn.t: Critics hail "War Horse" as a theatrical triumph, with its stunning life-size horse puppetry earning near-universal praise. Most find it emotionally stirring and visually spectacular, though a few dismiss it as overly sentimental.
